questions.question: The Cournot duopoly, in which each firm chooses a quantity from $[0,\infty)$, has a Nash equilibrium. What does this show about the finiteness assumption of the Nash existence theorem?
options: Finiteness is necessary, so the Cournot equilibrium must be in mixed strategies.
Finiteness can be dropped from the theorem: every game has an equilibrium.
Finiteness is irrelevant, since the theorem concerns only pure strategies.
Finiteness is sufficient for existence but not necessary.

questions.question: Why does the Nash existence theorem need mixed strategies rather than only pure strategies?
options: Finite games, such as Matching Pennies, can lack pure equilibria.
Mixed strategies give players higher payoffs than pure ones, which existence requires.
Mixed strategies are needed only to make the number of equilibria finite.
With pure strategies the best-response correspondence is always empty.

questions.question: In a Cournot duopoly the best-response functions are $BR_1(q_2)=\tfrac{90-q_2}{2}$ and $BR_2(q_1)=\tfrac{90-q_1}{2}$ (for $q_j\le90$). Which profile $(q_1,q_2)$ consists of mutual best responses?

By the Nash existence theorem a finite game has an equilibrium $\sigma^*$. Which property must every pure strategy $s_i$ that $\sigma_i^*$ plays with positive probability have, against $\sigma_{-i}^*$?
options: It is a best reply to every strategy of the other players
It earns the same as the other used ones, possibly less than an unused one
It is played with the same probability as the other used ones
It earns the highest expected payoff available against $\sigma_{-i}^*$

questions.question: Two players each name a positive integer; whoever names the larger number gets $1$ from the other, and a tie pays $0$. Why does the Nash existence theorem not imply that this game has an equilibrium?
options: It does imply one: both naming the same number is an equilibrium with payoff $0$.
Each player has infinitely many strategies, so the theorem does not apply.
It does imply one, since the game has finitely many players and is zero-sum.
The payoffs are not bounded, so the theorem's continuity requirement fails.
